history.origins: Noms is a British Royal Navy card game tradition, also known as 'Small Ships Rules.' It represents the naval variant of Nomination Whist, distinct from other games using the same name. The secret partnership mechanic and no-shuffle rule reflect the unique conditions of shipboard play.
timeline: 19th-20th Century: Played aboard Royal Navy vessels
Mid-20th Century: Rules formalized as 'Small Ships Rules'
Present: Preserved by naval veterans and card game enthusiasts
history.cultural: Strong British naval tradition. The 'Small Ships Rules' name indicates its association with smaller naval vessels where crew size made 4-player games practical.
history.evolution: The game developed the secret partnership mechanic to add intrigue to shipboard entertainment. The no-shuffle rule may have originated from limited playing space or superstition.

setup.players: 4 players. Partnerships are secret and determined by card nomination.
setup.dealing: 13 cards each, dealt in packets (4-3 pattern rotating). Cards are NOT shuffled between handsâ€”only cut.

rules.objective: Bidding team: win at least the bid number of tricks. Secret partnership revealed during play when nominated card is played.
rules.gameplay: If all pass, next hand is 'double hand' (stakes doubled). Follow suit if possible. Standard trick-taking rules apply.
keyRules: Cards NOT shuffled between handsâ€”only cut
Winner nominates a card to determine secret partner
All pass = double hand next round

strategy.basic: Bid with strong hands. As declarer, nominate a card you hold (for solo) or that you believe a strong opponent holds (to make them your partner).
strategy.intermediate: The no-shuffle rule means card memory is crucialâ€”track which cards were played in previous hands. Use this knowledge to nominate cards strategically.
strategy.advanced: Bluffing and deduction. As a defender, try to deduce who the secret partner is from the bidding and early play. Coordinate with your unknown partner without explicit communication.
tips: Remember: NO shufflingâ€”card memory is everything
Nominating an Ace or King you don't hold is risky; partner might be weak in that suit
MisÃ¨re is powerful when you have a very weak hand
Watch for tells when the secret partner is revealed

scoring.description: Stake-based. Successful contract: declarer 2 stakes, partner 1. Failed contract: opponents get 1 each from declarer/partner. Solo: 8 stakes.
